name: Dream Lands
lines: A pale lily-like flower of the Asphodel Meadows (real asphodel grows wild round the Mediterranean).
A small silver coin of ancient Greece. The dead were buried with one, for the ferryman.
From Persephone's tree. Hundreds of seeds, each in its own jewel of juice.
Pressed at the shade market.
In the old story the Sibyl calmed Cerberus with a honey cake. This one is for you.
Lantern of the shades
A keepsake: a little lantern with a pale, steady flame.
A tuft of cloud, soft and cool. It does not melt in the hand, in a dream.
Shed by a pegasus in flight.
Dew gathered on the cloud lawns at first light.
Light as air and baked on the cloud lawns.
Sweet, golden, served in a small cup.
A keepsake: a lap harp of twelve strings.
A keepsake: a ring of glass that catches the light.
Cut from a golden feather by the Gatekeeper himself.
Made by an oyster coating a grain of grit with nacre, layer on layer.
Glass rounded and frosted by the sea.
A great brown seaweed. People in many coastal countries eat it.
Crisp, salty, from the reef market.
Made by the merfolk from sea grapes, a real seaweed.
A keepsake: hold it to your ear and hear the sea (in fact, the air moving inside it).
A keepsake: a string of the Depths' own pearls.
Shell of the Queen's crown
A keepsake from Queen Maren, for the pearls you brought.
Petals that open only under the moon in Faerie.
Red with white spots. Real ones like it are poisonous: look, never eat.
An oak's seed. The gnomes store them for the winter.
Moonlight in a jar
A keepsake: it glows softly, and never flickers.
Dew in an acorn cup
Fairy fare. Very small.
From the bees of the elven tree.
A keepsake: tie it to a branch and make a small wish.
Dust from old stars. Much of the iron in your blood was made in stars.
Hold it close and it gives back the last thing you said.
Baked by the Lamplighter, in the shape of a star.
Warm, from the kettle in the lighthouse.
A keepsake: a brass lantern that always finds the way.
A keepsake: it points to the nearest light.
A piece of looking-glass. Its reflection is a moment late.
Fallen from the giant board. The Red Queen wants them back.
Grows in the looking-glass gardens.
The White Queen's rule: jam tomorrow, never today. This one you may eat today.
Poured from the cup into the pot.
Silver hand mirror
Travelling chess set
A keepsake: a folding board with all thirty-two pieces.
Cempasúchil, the flower of the Day of the Dead. Its petals make paths for the visiting souls.
Left on an ofrenda, still good for lighting.
A tree resin burned as incense on Mexican altars since long before the Spanish came.
The sweet bread of the Day of the Dead, with bones of dough across the top.
Thick hot chocolate made with corn masa.
A keepsake: decorated for an ofrenda, not for eating.
Papel picado banner
A keepsake: tissue paper cut in lacy patterns.
Six-sided, as every snow crystal is.
An orange berry of the Arctic bogs.
Shed on the snowfields at the end of winter.
Caught through the ice and smoked in the village.
Hot cloudberry tea
Warms you through.
A keepsake, and warm.
A keepsake: the ice palace under glass. Shake it gently.
It gives off a steady green light, as some real mushrooms and plankton do.
Light enough to bob a little when you let it go.
Grown under the great dome.
Baked in the settlement.
Bubbling spring water
From a spring under the domes.
Floating pebble in a jar
A keepsake: a sky-stone that hovers above the jar's floor.
Print of the twin moons
A keepsake: the two moons over the domes.
Volcanic glass: lava that cooled too fast to form crystals.
Yellow crystals from the volcano's vents.
The dwarf smiths bake it on the forge's hearthstone.
From a spring under the mountain, the coldest thing in the Burning Lands.
A keepsake, knapped by a dwarf smith.
A keepsake from the Phoenix: warm to the touch, never hot.
Most meteorites are stone; some are iron and nickel.
Light gathered from old stars.
Comets are made of ice and dust. Ice in space could one day be water and rocket fuel.
Freeze-dried ice cream
Crunchy. Sold to visitors more than it was ever eaten in space.
Drunk through a straw, as in orbit.
A keepsake: the stars as seen from here.
Brass pocket telescope
Seeds are worth most in Haven: things grow again.
Collected for recycling: batteries never belong in the ground.
From the soup kitchen. Bean and whatever-we-grew-this-week.
Filtered through sand and charcoal, then boiled.
A keepsake: a lantern made from a tin can.
A keepsake: a sunflower welded from scrap.
From the oasis palms.
Real: a rosette of gypsum crystals that forms in dry, salty sand.
A piece of an old water jar, worn smooth by the sand.
Hot, sweet and poured from high up.
Flatbread with dates
Baked on hot stones at the caravan camp.
A pinch of saffron
The threads of a crocus flower, picked by hand.
A keepsake. Rubbing it does nothing at all.
In orbit a lost bolt drifts away; aboard, it rolls under a console.
Turns sunlight straight into electricity.
From the station's grow-racks, under LED light.
Heated in its pouch.
With a straw that clips shut.
A keepsake: every crew designs its own.
Model of the Orbital
From the farms on the tower roofs.
Glass, metal and paper, kept apart so each can be made new.
A light that uses a fraction of an old bulb's power.
From the coffee cart on the plaza.
Grown forty floors up.
Print of the City to Come
From the trees along the Row.
Clay tablet fragment
Pressed with wedge-shaped marks: cuneiform, the oldest writing we know.
From the pilgrims' stall.
From the fountain court's spring.
Guidebook to the Row
A keepsake: every house on the Row, and what its parts are for.
Your name in cuneiform
A keepsake: the scribe pressed your name into clay.
Stamped in all sixteen dream lands. The Registrar of Doors signed it.
Charon the ferryman
The ferryman's fare
Coins fall from the shades' pockets all along the road. Bring me five obols and I'll carry the next five who can't pay.
Seeds for the spring
When I go up, I take the spring with me. Bring me asphodel and two of my pomegranates, and the meadows above will bloom early.
A posy for the fields
Nothing pale grows in Elysium. Bring eight asphodel and we'll plant them by the river, so the newcomers see something they know.
The shade at the stall
The Road of Shades
Run the road from my jetty to the Elysian Fields before the lamps go down. Through every ring.
The judges' questions
Three questions on the old stories. Answer all three truly.
Who ferried the dead across the River Styx?
How many heads did Cerberus have, in most of the old stories?
Why did Persephone have to stay in the Underworld part of every year?
She ate pomegranate seeds there
She lost a bet with Hades
She missed the last ferry
Which river made the dead forget their lives?
Which musician sang his way into the Underworld to bring back his wife?
Where did the blessed heroes rest?
The Elysian Fields
The Asphodel Meadows
a gentle shade who keeps a little stall of juice, honey cakes and lanterns by the road to the Hall of Judgement
Something for the road, traveller? Juice from the queen's own tree, and honey cakes. The dog likes them too.
Quills for the book
Every dreamer's name goes in the book, and my quills wear down. Three golden feathers, if you find them: the pegasi drop them east of the gate.
We write every kindness in ink made with morning dew. Five drops, from the lawns round the fountain.
Cushions for the choir
The palace steps are hard on old knees. Eight tufts of cloud wool would make cushions for the whole choir.
The cloud-baker's stall
Carry a message from the gate to the palace steps and round by the stair. Through every ring, and quickly.
The harpist's pairs
Turn two cards at a time and find each instrument's pair.
a cheerful baker who bakes cloud bread on the cloud lawns and sells nectar by the fountain court
Fresh from the cloud oven! Light as air, and it fills you up all the same. A cup of nectar with it?
Queen Maren of the Depths
Pearls for the crown
My crown lost three pearls in the last great storm. The oyster beds on the reef might give you three more.
Glass for the lanterns
Sea glass makes the prettiest lanterns on the reef. Six pieces, any colour.
A diver from the surface
Samples for the surface
I'd love samples to take back up: four fronds of kelp and two bits of sea glass. Kelp forests are among the fastest-growing things in the sea.
Ride the reef current round the market and the wreck. Through every ring.
The Queen's questions
Tell me true things about your oceans, and I will tell you true things about mine.
About how deep does sunlight reach in the open ocean?
What is the deepest place known in the oceans?
The Challenger Deep
The Great Barrier Reef
How does an oyster make a pearl?
It coats a bit of grit with nacre
It swallows a white stone
It grows one every spring
Colonies of tiny animals
A kind of rock that grows
How much of the Earth's surface does the ocean cover?
What do whales breathe?
Air, at the surface
Water, through gills
Nothing; they hold it for life
Petals for the bower
My bower wants petals, and the moon petals are the softest. Eight, from anywhere in the wood.
Toadstools for a new ring
A fairy ring grows outward, year on year. Help it along: five toadstools, and I'll set them where the next ring will be.
A gnome of the village
Winter's coming to the toadstool village, even in Faerie. Ten acorns would fill my larder.
Find the hidden pixies
Six pixies are hiding in the wood. Walk up to each one and it will light up. Find them all before the moon moves on.
Answer three riddles, mortal, and I'll grant you a small bargain: gold, and nothing tricky.
I have roots that no one sees, I'm taller than the tallest trees, up I go and yet I never grow. What am I?
The more of me you take, the more you leave behind. What am I?
I have a ring but no finger, I grow at night and vanish by day. What am I?
A fairy ring of mushrooms
What has hands but cannot clap?
I'm light as a feather, yet the strongest can't hold me long. What am I?
What can run but never walks, has a mouth but never talks?
The lamp burns stardust here, nothing else will do. Six handfuls and it will burn another age.
Crystals for the lens
The great lens has a crack. Two star crystals from the spire would mend it.
What the stones remember
The echo stones hold the last words said near them. Bring me four; I keep a record of what the lost have said.
The lighthouse kitchen
Relight the beacons
Six beacons mark the ways back. They have gone out. Walk to each and it will light again, before the dark closes in.
Pieces for the board
Pieces keep wandering off the board. Bring me four, at once! Well, as soon as you can run there and back.
Mend tomorrow's mirror
I shall break my mirror tomorrow, you know, so I'm mending it today. Five shards, please.
Roses for both of us
Six roses: three for me and three for my reflection. Or is it the other way round?
The looking-glass shop
Every card has its twin. Turn two at a time and find them all.
The Red Queen's questions
Questions! Quickly! Off with the wrong answers.
What does a mirror really swap?
How many squares are on a chessboard?
In chess, what can a pawn become if it reaches the far side?
Any piece but a king
Which word reads the same backwards?
Who wrote Through the Looking-Glass?
Hans Christian Andersen
The Brothers Grimm
What is the coating behind a glass mirror usually made of?
A thin layer of silver or aluminium
the Land of the Dead
The Lantern Keeper
Light for the remembered
Six candles, and six more souls will have a light to find their way home by.
A skeleton fiddler
The petals make a path from the graveyard to the ofrendas, so the visitors don't get lost. Ten marigolds would do it.
Copal for the ofrenda
The ofrenda wants copal for its smoke and marigolds for its colour. Four of each.
The baker of the ofrendas
Light the lanterns
Eight lanterns stand dark tonight. Walk up to each and light it before the bells ring.
a baker who keeps the stall among the market tables, selling pan de muerto, champurrado, sugar skulls and papel picado
Pan de muerto, still warm! And champurrado to go with it. Take a sugar skull for your ofrenda, too.
The Steward of the Ice Palace
The north wind chipped the palace windows. Six ice crystals will mend them before the Queen comes home.
Berries for the village
Cloudberries keep all winter in a cold cellar. Six would see my family through to spring.
Wool for the yurts
The mammoths shed in tufts. Five of them and I can felt a new wall for the yurt.
The ice fisher's stall
Skate the frozen lake: through every ring before the sun goes behind the palace.
A trader of the domes
A stone that floats
Sky-stones fetch a good price at home. Four, and I'll pay you well.
Fruit for the seed bank
We keep a seed from every fruit, in case the dome ever fails. Five dome fruit, please.
Moss for the lamps
Glow moss lights the settlement at night without a spark of power. Eight clumps.
The settlement market
Wake the monoliths
The ring of monoliths by the moon pool sleeps. Touch each one and it wakes. All seven, before it dozes off again.
The skyport warden
Fly the skyport loop on foot: round the landing pads and the domes, through every ring.
the warden of the skyport, where ships from other worlds set down
Mind the pad, a ship's due. Visitors from three worlds came through today. Shall I show you the loop the pilots walk to check the pads?
Where ships from other worlds set down
Ships land on a pad ringed with lights, as helicopters do on Earth.
The habitats beside it are for crews waiting for fair weather.
On a planet with thinner air, wings give less lift, so ships here land straight down.
A smith of the forges
Embers for the forge
The great forge eats emberstone. Four, from the ember fields, and you can work at it yourself.
Obsidian for the windows
The palace windows are cut from obsidian, polished thin. Five pieces, please; the black ones shine best.
The forge-side stall
Samples for the lab
Light for the spectrometer
The pilot's locker
The astronomer's sky quiz
